Three papers in the library propose and test a fix for lost-in-the-middle. Each one changes a different part of the system: the **prompt**, the **attention at inference time**, or the **training data**. Page numbers are PDF page numbers.

### 1. LongLLMLingua — reorders the prompt (`llm/context/`)
- **Problem it targets:** It names position bias ("lost in the middle") as one of three problems with long contexts, alongside cost and noise (p. 1). Document reordering is one of its five contributions, there to "minimize position bias" (p. 1).
- **What it changes:** In §4.2, "How to reduce information loss in the middle?", it takes the documents left after coarse-grained compression and sorts them by their question-relevance scores, most important first (p. 4).
- **Effect:** In the ablation, the version with reordering scores 76.2 whichever position the answer document is in (p. 8). The appendix says reordering "can effectively alleviate the 'lost in the middle' issue," even on tasks where order matters, like timeline reordering (p. 14, p. 16).

### 2. Found in the Middle — recalibrates attention, no retraining (`llm/context/`)
- **Diagnosis:** Models give more attention to tokens at the start and end of the input, "regardless of their relevance," in a U-shape. The authors trace lost-in-the-middle to this bias (p. 1, p. 4).
- **What it changes:** It models attention as relevance plus a positional bias (Eq. 2, p. 5). It estimates the bias by putting a dummy document at the same position and subtracting its attention, which gives "calibrated attention" (p. 5–6). It then rescales the attention on each document's tokens so the total attention on that document follows a softmax of its relevance, with a temperature t (Eq. 5–6, p. 6).
- **Effect:** Gains of up to 15 percentage points over the uncalibrated model, and 6–15 points when the gold document is in the middle (p. 7). It also works on top of reordering methods such as LongLLMLingua, and that combination scored best (p. 7–8). The authors say reordering alone depends on ranking the documents correctly and doesn't remove the model's built-in bias (p. 2, p. 7).

### 3. Make Your LLM Fully Utilize the Context (IN2 / FILM-7B) — changes the training data (`llm/context/`)
- **Diagnosis:** Ordinary training data quietly teaches a position bias. Next-token loss depends mostly on nearby tokens, and system messages usually come at the start (p. 2).
- **What it changes:** "INformation-INtensive" (IN2) training, described as "a purely data-driven solution" (p. 1). It fine-tunes on synthetic long-context QA built from about 128-token segments placed at random in contexts of 4K–32K tokens. Some questions need one segment; others need reasoning across two or more segments far apart (p. 2–4). Context lengths are spread evenly, and about 10% short-context data is kept so the model doesn't forget short-context skills (p. 4).
- **Effect:** Applied to Mistral-7B, the resulting FILM-7B retrieves information reliably from any position in its 32K window. NarrativeQA F1 went from 23.5 to 26.9, and MMLU stayed about the same (59.3 → 59.2) (p. 1–2).

### Papers that only test or suggest fixes
- **Lost in the Middle** (Liu et al.) tested "query-aware contextualization," which puts the query both before and after the documents. It nearly solved the synthetic key-value task but "minimally affects" multi-document QA (p. 8). The paper treats this as an investigation of causes, not a proposed remedy (p. 7).
- **Retrieval meets Long Context LLMs** confirms the effect in Llama2-70B (p. 7). It calls mitigation "an open research topic" and suggests that continued pretraining with the UL2 loss "could be one potential solution," without testing it (p. 9).

Many other papers in the library mention lost-in-the-middle only as motivation (for example LightMem p. 1 and MemDefrag p. 1). They don't propose a fix aimed at it, so I left them out.
